topics.name: Naming words: noun, verb, adjective and more
Pronoun forms: I and me, myself
Should have, must have, might have
Words for cooking, sport and yoga
What speech shows about a person

items.sentence: My brother plays football.
items.rule: A sentence starts with a capital letter and ends with a full stop.

items.sentence: We live in India.
items.rule: Names of places start with a capital letter.

items.sentence: I saw [a] elephant at the zoo.
items.rule: Use "an" before a vowel sound: an elephant.

items.sentence: She has [an] red umbrella.
items.rule: Use "a" before a consonant sound: a red umbrella.

items.sentence: He ate [a] apple after lunch.
items.rule: Use "an" before a vowel sound: an apple.

items.sentence: There are three [box] on the table.
items.rule: Words ending in x take -es: boxes.

items.sentence: The two [baby] are sleeping.
items.rule: Change y to ies: baby, babies.

items.sentence: I brushed my [tooths] this morning.
items.rule: Tooth is irregular: one tooth, two teeth.

items.sentence: Ravi is my friend. [She] is ten years old.
items.rule: Ravi is a boy, so the pronoun is "he".

items.sentence: The girls lost [her] ball.
items.rule: "The girls" is plural, so use "their".

items.sentence: Give the book to [I].
items.rule: After "to", use "me".

items.sentence: Where do you live?
items.rule: A question starts with a question word and ends with a question mark.

items.sentence: Can you swim?
items.rule: In a question the helping verb comes first.

items.sentence: Ravi has a blue bag.
items.rule: A name starts with a capital letter, and the sentence ends with a full stop.

items.sentence: On Monday we go to school.
items.rule: Names of days start with a capital letter.

items.sentence: My uncle bought [a] umbrella.
items.rule: Use "an" before a vowel sound: an umbrella.

items.sentence: There is [an] cat on the wall.
items.rule: Use "a" before a consonant sound: a cat.

items.sentence: We saw two [bus] at the stop.
items.rule: Words ending in s take -es: buses.

items.sentence: The [childs] are playing outside.
items.rule: Child is irregular: one child, two children.

items.sentence: What is your name?
items.rule: A question starts with a question word and ends with a question mark.

items.sentence: Is this your pencil?
items.rule: In a question the verb "is" comes first.

items.sentence: Meena has a doll. [He] plays with it every day.
items.rule: Meena is a girl, so the pronoun is "she".

items.sentence: The dog sleeps under the table.
items.rule: A noun names a person, animal, place or thing: dog, table.

items.sentence: My sister sings well.
items.rule: A noun names a person, animal, place or thing: sister.

items.sentence: Ravi kicked the ball.
items.rule: A noun names a person, animal, place or thing: ball. A name such as Ravi is a noun too.

items.sentence: The teacher opened a window.
items.rule: A noun names a person, animal, place or thing: teacher, window.

items.sentence: The baby laughed loudly.
items.rule: A verb tells what someone or something does: laughed.

items.sentence: Birds fly over our house.
items.rule: A verb tells what someone or something does: fly.

items.sentence: Meena reads a story every night.
items.rule: A verb tells what someone or something does: reads.

items.sentence: We played cricket yesterday.
items.rule: A verb tells what someone or something does: played.

items.sentence: ant bat cat dog
items.rule: Words go in the order of their first letters: ant, bat, cat, dog.
items.task: Tap the words in alphabetical order.

items.sentence: egg fan goat hen
items.rule: Words go in the order of their first letters: egg, fan, goat, hen.

items.rule: Words go in the order of their first letters: kite, lamp, moon, nest.

items.sentence: The dogs [is] barking loudly.
items.rule: A plural subject takes "are": the dogs are.

items.sentence: My sister [like] mangoes.
items.rule: With he, she or one person, add -s: she likes.

items.sentence: We [was] late for school.
items.rule: "We" takes "were".

items.sentence: Yesterday we [play] cricket.
items.rule: "Yesterday" needs the past: played.

items.sentence: She [goed] to the market.
items.rule: Go is irregular: go, went.

items.sentence: I [eated] two idlis.
items.rule: Eat is irregular: eat, ate.

items.sentence: The books are [in] the table.
items.rule: Things rest on a table.

items.sentence: We go to school [in] Monday.
items.rule: Use "on" with days: on Monday.

items.sentence: He was born [on] March.
items.rule: Use "in" with months: in March.

items.sentence: I like tea and coffee.
items.rule: "And" joins two things.

items.sentence: He ran fast but missed the bus.
items.rule: "But" joins two ideas that do not match.

items.sentence: We read The Jungle [book] in class.
items.rule: The main words in a title start with capital letters.

items.sentence: My favourite story is The Clever [crow].
items.rule: The main words in a title start with capital letters.

items.sentence: Our class is reading Malgudi [days] this term.
items.rule: The main words in a title start with capital letters.

items.sentence: The [dogs] tail is wagging; our dog is happy.
items.rule: For one owner, add an apostrophe and s: the dog's tail.

items.sentence: I borrowed my [sisters] pen; I have one sister.
items.rule: For one owner, add an apostrophe and s: my sister's pen.

items.sentence: There are three [dog's] in the park.
items.rule: A plural needs no apostrophe: three dogs.

items.sentence: You can have milk or juice.
items.rule: "Or" joins two choices.

items.sentence: She was tired, so she went to bed.
items.rule: "So" shows the result.

items.sentence: Last night it [rain] heavily.
items.rule: "Last night" needs the past: rained.

items.sentence: We [see] a rainbow yesterday.
items.rule: See is irregular: see, saw.

items.sentence: We visited our aunt last week.
items.rule: For something that is over, use the past: visited.

items.sentence: He [have] two brothers.
items.rule: With he, she or one person, use "has".

items.sentence: The cat is under the table.
items.rule: A preposition shows where: under the table.

items.sentence: Yesterday I helped my father.
items.rule: "Yesterday" needs the past: helped.

items.sentence: My sisters are at home.
items.rule: A plural subject takes "are": my sisters are.

items.sentence: The tall boy carried a heavy bag.
items.rule: An adjective describes a noun: tall boy, heavy bag.

items.sentence: She wore a red dress.
items.rule: An adjective describes a noun: red dress.

items.sentence: The old man told a funny story.
items.rule: An adjective describes a noun: old man, funny story.

items.sentence: Ravi lost the pen, but he found it later.
items.rule: A pronoun stands in place of a noun: he for Ravi, it for the pen.

items.sentence: The girls said they were hungry.
items.rule: A pronoun stands in place of a noun: they for the girls.

items.sentence: The soup is hot.
items.rule: Is, am, are, was and were are verbs too.

items.sentence: The old dog barked loudly.
items.rule: The subject is who or what the sentence is about: the old dog. The rest of the sentence, which tells about the subject, is the predicate.

items.sentence: My sister sings every morning.
items.rule: The subject is who or what the sentence is about: my sister. The rest of the sentence, which tells about the subject, is the predicate.

items.sentence: Birds fly south in winter.
items.rule: The subject is who or what the sentence is about: birds. The rest of the sentence, which tells about the subject, is the predicate.

items.sentence: The little boy lost a shoe.
items.rule: The subject is who or what the sentence is about: the little boy. The rest of the sentence, which tells about the subject, is the predicate.

items.sentence: A [herd] of bees flew past the window.
items.rule: A group of bees is a swarm.

items.sentence: We saw a [flock] of lions at the zoo.
items.rule: A group of lions is a pride.

items.sentence: A [bunch] of wolves howled at night.
items.rule: A group of wolves is a pack.

items.sentence: She bought a [pack] of bananas.
items.rule: Bananas come in a bunch.

items.sentence: The ring is made of [wood] and shines like the sun.
items.rule: A material noun names what a thing is made of: gold.

items.sentence: [A] sun rises in the east.
items.rule: Use the for a thing there is only one of: the sun.

items.sentence: I saw a dog in the lane. [A] dog was barking.
items.rule: Use the when the thing has already been mentioned: the dog.

items.sentence: She is [the] honest girl.
items.rule: Use an before a vowel sound, when you mean any one of a kind: an honest girl.

items.sentence: How [many] water is in the jug?
items.rule: Water cannot be counted, so use much: how much water.

items.sentence: She bought some [breads] from the shop.
items.rule: Bread cannot be counted, so it has no plural: some bread.

items.sentence: How [much] apples are in the basket?
items.rule: Apples can be counted, so use many: how many apples.

items.sentence: My friend lives in [chennai].
items.rule: The name of a place is a proper noun and starts with a capital letter.

items.sentence: We met [ravi] at the park.
items.rule: The name of a person is a proper noun and starts with a capital letter.

items.sentence: The old dog barked loudly.
items.rule: The predicate tells what the subject does or is: barked loudly.

items.sentence: My sister sings every morning.
items.rule: The predicate tells what the subject does or is: sings every morning.

items.sentence: Birds fly south in winter.
items.rule: The predicate tells what the subject does or is: fly south in winter.

items.sentence: Tomorrow we will [went] to the zoo.
items.rule: After will, use the plain verb: will go.

items.sentence: Next week she will [visits] her aunt.
items.rule: After will, use the plain verb: will visit.

items.sentence: I will [helped] you after lunch.
items.rule: After will, use the plain verb: will help.

items.sentence: We stayed inside because it was raining.
items.rule: "Because" gives the reason.

items.sentence: Although he was tired, he finished his homework.
items.rule: "Although" joins two ideas that seem to pull apart.

items.sentence: I was hungry, [but] I ate a sandwich.
items.rule: "So" shows the result.

items.sentence: Take an umbrella [so] it may rain.
items.rule: "Because" gives the reason.

items.sentence: Hurray! We have won the match.
items.rule: An interjection shows sudden feeling and takes an exclamation mark.

items.sentence: Oh no! I forgot my lunch box.
items.rule: An interjection shows sudden feeling: here, dismay.

items.sentence: Wow! What a beautiful rainbow!
items.rule: "Wow" shows wonder.

items.sentence: The [boys] room is upstairs; three boys share it.
items.rule: For a plural ending in s, the apostrophe comes after the s: boys'.

items.sentence: The [childrens] park is closed.
items.rule: "Children" is plural without s, so add 's.

items.sentence: This pencil is [my].
items.rule: When no noun follows, use "mine".

items.sentence: That house is [their].
items.rule: When no noun follows, use "theirs".

items.sentence: I [cant] find my shoes.
items.rule: The apostrophe stands for the missing letters: can't.

items.sentence: She [does'nt] like bitter gourd.
items.rule: The apostrophe replaces the o of "not": doesn't.

items.sentence: [Its] raining, so take an umbrella.
items.rule: "It's" means "it is".

items.sentence: They [wont] come to the party.
items.rule: "Will not" becomes "won't".

items.sentence: She [breaked] the glass yesterday.
items.rule: Break is irregular: break, broke, broken.

items.sentence: He has [ate] all the sweets.
items.rule: After has or have, use the third form: eaten.

items.sentence: We [buyed] vegetables from the market.
items.rule: Buy is irregular: buy, bought.

items.sentence: The bell has already [rang].
items.rule: Ring, rang, rung: after "has" use rung.

items.sentence: Each of the boys [have] a bat.
items.rule: "Each" is singular: each has.

items.sentence: The news [are] good today.
items.rule: "News" is singular.

items.sentence: My friends and I [am] going to the fair.
items.rule: People joined by "and" take "are".

items.sentence: I wanted to play, but it was too dark.
items.rule: Two simple sentences joined by "but" make a compound sentence.

items.sentence: She opened the door and the cat ran out.
items.rule: "And" joins two simple sentences into a compound sentence.

items.sentence: You can walk or you can take the bus.
items.rule: "Or" joins two choices.

items.sentence: What a lovely day it is!
items.rule: An exclamation ends with an exclamation mark.

items.sentence: My birthday is in [july].
items.rule: Months start with a capital letter.

items.sentence: We visited [delhi] last winter.
items.rule: Names of places start with a capital letter.

items.sentence: Yes, I have finished my work.
items.rule: A comma follows "yes" or "no" at the start of an answer.

items.sentence: The tortoise walked slowly.
items.rule: An adverb tells how, when or where something is done: slowly tells how it walked.

items.sentence: She answered the question correctly.
items.rule: An adverb tells how, when or where something is done: correctly tells how she answered.

items.sentence: We will leave tomorrow.
items.rule: An adverb tells how, when or where something is done: tomorrow tells when.

items.sentence: The cat jumped over the wall.
items.rule: A preposition shows where or when one thing is in relation to another: over the wall.

items.sentence: He kept the keys in a drawer.
items.rule: A preposition shows where or when one thing is in relation to another: in a drawer.

items.sentence: Meena filled the kettle. She waited for the water to boil. Then she poured the tea.
items.rule: Words such as then show what comes later.
parts: She waited for the water to boil.

items.sentence: First, wash the rice. Next, boil it in a pot of water. Finally, serve it hot.
items.rule: First, next and finally show the order of the steps.
parts: Next, boil it in a pot of water.

items.sentence: The sky grew dark. Soon it began to rain. After the rain, a rainbow appeared.
items.rule: Soon and after show what follows.
parts: After the rain, a rainbow appeared.

items.sentence: Ravi woke up late. He ran to the bus stop. Sadly, the bus had already left. So he walked to school.
items.rule: Each sentence leads to the next: late, so he ran; the bus had left, so he walked.
parts: He ran to the bus stop.
Sadly, the bus had already left.

items.sentence: He is as busy as a [cat].
items.rule: A simile compares with as or like. The usual one is: as busy as a bee.

items.sentence: The baby's blanket was as soft as [stone].
items.rule: A simile compares two things that share a quality: as soft as silk.

items.sentence: She ran as fast as a [snail].
items.rule: A simile must fit: a fast runner is like a fast animal, such as a deer.

items.sentence: The night was as black as [milk].
items.rule: A simile must fit: as black as coal.

items.sentence: The tired boy [danced] slowly up the steep hill.
items.rule: Choose the action word that fits: a tired boy walks or climbs.

items.sentence: She was [sad] when she won the first prize.
items.rule: Choose the feeling word that fits: winning makes you happy.

items.sentence: The hungry lion [whispered] loudly in its cage.
items.rule: Choose the sound word that fits: a lion roars.

items.sentence: He [shouted] softly so that the baby would not wake.
items.rule: Choose the word that fits softly: whispered.

items.sentence: After walking all day without food, the boys were famished.
items.question: What does "famished" most likely mean here?
items.rule: Walking all day without food points to hunger.

items.sentence: The path was so narrow that only one person could walk on it at a time.
items.question: What does "narrow" most likely mean here?
items.rule: Only one person could walk on it, so it was not wide.

items.sentence: She sings [beautiful].
items.rule: An adverb of manner tells how: beautifully.

items.sentence: He ran [quick] to the gate.
items.rule: An adverb of manner often ends in -ly: quickly.

items.sentence: We often play chess in the evening.
items.rule: An adverb of frequency such as "often" goes before the main verb.

items.sentence: The children are playing outside.
items.rule: An adverb of place tells where: outside.

items.sentence: The train arrives [on] six o'clock.
items.rule: Use "at" with clock times.

items.sentence: She is good [in] drawing.
items.rule: We say "good at".

items.sentence: He divided the sweets [between] the five children.
items.rule: Use "among" for more than two; "between" for two.

items.sentence: We walked [between] the forest for an hour.
items.rule: "Through" means from one side of something to the other.

items.sentence: Please look [on] this word in the dictionary.
items.rule: "Look up" means to find information.

items.sentence: Please turn [of] the lights when you leave.
items.rule: "Turn off" means to stop a light or machine.

items.sentence: We must not give [in] hope.
items.rule: "Give up" means to stop trying or let go.

items.sentence: A stitch in time saves nine.
items.rule: It means: fix a small problem now, before it grows.

items.sentence: Actions speak louder than words.
items.rule: It means: what you do matters more than what you say.

items.sentence: Honesty is the best policy.
items.rule: It means: it is always better to tell the truth.

items.sentence: Ravi is [tall] than his brother.
items.rule: To compare two, add -er: taller than.

items.sentence: This is the [better] book in the library.
items.rule: To compare more than two, use the superlative: best.

items.sentence: She runs [fast] than her sister.
items.rule: To compare two actions, add -er: faster than.

items.sentence: This puzzle is [difficulter] than the last one.
items.rule: Long adjectives take "more": more difficult.

items.sentence: Look! The baby is [sleep].
items.rule: The continuous tense is "is" with verb-ing.

items.sentence: They were [swim] when it started to rain.
items.rule: The past continuous is "were" with verb-ing.

items.sentence: She was writing a letter when the phone rang.
items.rule: The past continuous shows an action going on when another happened.

items.sentence: I am [writeing] a story.
items.rule: Drop the e before -ing: writing.

items.sentence: "Where are you going?" asked Ravi.
items.rule: Spoken words go inside quotation marks, with their own question mark.

items.sentence: Meena said, "I am hungry."
items.rule: A comma comes before the spoken words; the full stop stays inside the marks.

items.sentence: First I brushed my teeth, and then I went to bed.
items.rule: Linking words such as "first" and "then" show the order.

items.sentence: Finally, we reached the top of the hill.
items.rule: "Finally" marks the last event.

items.sentence: "Come here," said Mother.
items.rule: The spoken words go inside quotation marks, with a comma before the closing mark.

items.sentence: "I won!" shouted Arun.
items.rule: The exclamation mark belongs to the spoken words, so it stays inside the marks.

items.sentence: Father asked, "Who broke the window?"
items.rule: A comma comes before the spoken words; their question mark stays inside the marks.

items.sentence: I was tired, but I finished the work.
items.rule: A conjunction joins words or parts of a sentence: but.

items.sentence: We stayed inside because the rain was heavy.
items.rule: A conjunction joins words or parts of a sentence: because.

items.sentence: Honesty is a good habit.
items.rule: Some nouns name ideas you cannot touch: honesty, habit.

items.sentence: The children were happy.
items.rule: An adjective can come after is, are, was or were: the children were happy.

items.sentence: The bus has reached the station.
items.rule: A verb can be two words: has reached.

items.sentence: It was raining cats and [mice].
items.rule: Raining cats and dogs means raining very hard.

items.sentence: The test was a piece of [bread].
items.rule: A piece of cake means very easy.

items.sentence: Hold your [donkeys], I am coming.
items.rule: Hold your horses means wait a moment.

items.sentence: She let the cat out of the [box].
items.rule: To let the cat out of the bag means to tell a secret by mistake.

items.sentence: Mother [boiled] the cake in the oven.
items.rule: In cooking, a cake is baked in an oven.

items.sentence: The batsman hit the ball and scored four [goals].
items.rule: In cricket, a batsman scores runs.

items.sentence: The referee blew his [bell] to start the match.
items.rule: A referee uses a whistle.

items.sentence: Sit on your yoga [carpet] and cross your legs.
items.rule: Yoga is done on a mat.

items.sentence: In yoga we breathe in deeply and then breathe [up].
items.rule: The opposite of breathe in is breathe out.

items.sentence: I think reading is fun because stories take me to new places.
items.rule: An opinion is stronger with a reason. Because joins the two.

items.sentence: In my opinion, we should plant trees since they give shade.
items.rule: Since can give the reason for an opinion.

items.sentence: I like mangoes more than apples because they are sweeter.
items.rule: Because gives the reason for what you like.

items.sentence: Cycling keeps us fit, so I ride to school.
items.rule: So joins a reason to what follows from it.

items.sentence: The bees [roared] around the hive.
items.rule: Some words sound like what they name: bees buzz.

items.sentence: The snake [barked] in the long grass.
items.rule: Some words sound like what they name: a snake hisses.

items.sentence: The old door [sang] as it opened.
items.rule: Some words sound like what they name: an old door creaks.

items.sentence: She has three pens.
items.question: What kind of adjective is "three"?
items.rule: An adjective of number tells how many: three pens.

items.sentence: He lives in a small house.
items.question: What kind of adjective is "small"?
items.rule: An adjective of quality tells what kind: a small house.

items.sentence: This book is mine.
items.question: What kind of adjective is "This"?
items.rule: A demonstrative adjective points out which one: this book.

items.sentence: My bag is on the table.
items.question: What kind of adjective is "My"?
items.rule: A possessive adjective shows who owns a thing: my bag.

items.sentence: There is some milk in the jug.
items.question: What kind of adjective is "some"?
items.rule: An adjective of quantity tells how much: some milk.

items.sentence: The timid kitten hid under the bed whenever a visitor came.
items.question: What does "timid" most likely mean here?
items.rule: Hiding from visitors shows that it was easily frightened.

items.sentence: The old bridge was so fragile that the villagers crossed it one at a time.
items.question: What does "fragile" most likely mean here?
items.rule: They crossed one at a time for fear that it would break.

items.sentence: He drives very [careful] in the rain.
items.rule: "Very" can strengthen an adverb: very carefully.

items.sentence: Alas! The old tree has fallen.
items.rule: "Alas" shows sorrow.

items.sentence: She takes [up] her mother: they have the same smile.
items.rule: "Take after" means to be like an older family member.

items.sentence: The police will look [up] the matter.
items.rule: "Look into" means to examine.

items.sentence: Do not count your chickens before they hatch.
items.rule: It means: do not depend on something before it happens.

items.sentence: The dog wagged [it's] tail.
items.rule: "Its" shows belonging; "it's" means "it is".

items.sentence: Of all the singers, Meena sang the [more] sweetly.
items.rule: Of more than two, use "most".

items.sentence: I have never [saw] snow.
items.rule: See, saw, seen: after "have" use seen.

items.sentence: Neither of the answers [are] correct.
items.rule: "Neither" is singular.

items.sentence: One of my shoes [are] missing.
items.rule: The subject is "one", so the verb is singular.

items.sentence: He studied hard, so he passed the test.
items.rule: "So" joins a cause to its result.

items.sentence: After the rain stopped, the children went out to play.
items.rule: "After" shows which event came first.

items.sentence: Later that evening, we watched the fireworks.
items.rule: "Later" moves the story on in time.

items.sentence: My uncle, who lives in Pune, is a doctor.
items.rule: Commas go around extra information about a person.

items.sentence: I have [live] here for five years.
items.rule: After "have", use the third form: have lived.

items.sentence: We have [know] each other since class one.
items.rule: After "have", use the third form: know, knew, known.

items.sentence: She has been [wait] for an hour.
items.rule: "Has been" is followed by verb-ing.

items.sentence: [Their] is a parrot on the roof.
items.rule: "There is" points something out; "their" shows belonging.

items.sentence: I am taller [then] my cousin.
items.rule: "Than" compares; "then" is about time.

items.sentence: Please [except] my apology.
items.rule: "Accept" means to take; "except" means leaving out.

items.sentence: The box of mangoes [are] on the table.
items.rule: The subject is "box", not "mangoes", so the verb is singular.

items.sentence: The boys in the last row [is] talking.
items.rule: The subject is "boys", so the verb is plural.

items.sentence: By the time we arrived, the film had [start].
items.rule: The past perfect is "had" with the third form: had started.

items.sentence: They have [went] home.
items.rule: Go, went, gone: after "have" use gone.

items.sentence: First we mixed the flour, then we added water.
items.rule: "First" and "then" show the order of the steps.

items.sentence: I wanted to play, but it was too dark.
items.rule: "But" joins two sentences that pull apart; a comma comes before it.

items.sentence: She was [happy] to lose her favourite pen.
items.rule: The prefix un- means not: unhappy.

items.sentence: The magician made the coin [appear] into thin air.
items.rule: The prefix dis- gives the opposite: disappear.

items.sentence: He is a very [care] driver and has never had an accident.
items.rule: The suffix -ful means full of: careful.

items.sentence: The teacher asked me to [write] the untidy page again neatly.
items.rule: The prefix re- means again: rewrite.

items.sentence: The dirty water was not [drink].
items.rule: The suffix -able means can be: drinkable.

items.sentence: Ravi kicked the ball.
items.rule: Kicked is a transitive verb: it has an object, the ball. In "Ravi ran", ran has no object, so it is intransitive.

items.sentence: The girl opened the window.
items.rule: Opened is transitive here: its object is the window. In "The shop opened", there is no object.

items.sentence: My mother baked a cake yesterday.
items.rule: Baked is transitive: its object is a cake. Yesterday tells when; it is not an object.

items.sentence: The children sang a song loudly.
items.rule: Sang is transitive here: its object is a song. In "The children sang loudly", there is no object.

items.sentence: It rained heavily. However, the match went on.
items.rule: However joins two ideas that pull apart.

items.sentence: He practised daily. Therefore, he improved quickly.
items.rule: Therefore shows the result.

items.sentence: She was tired. [Therefore], she kept working.
items.rule: However shows that the second idea is unexpected.

items.sentence: The opposite of generous is [kind].
items.rule: An antonym is a word of opposite meaning: generous, mean.

items.sentence: A word that means the same as brave is [timid].
items.rule: A synonym is a word of the same meaning: brave, courageous.

items.sentence: Hot is to cold as day is to [sun].
items.rule: An analogy matches pairs: hot and cold are opposites, so are day and night.

items.sentence: The opposite of ancient is [old].
items.rule: An antonym is a word of opposite meaning: ancient, modern.

items.sentence: Glove is to hand as sock is to [shoe].
items.rule: An analogy matches pairs: a glove goes on a hand, a sock goes on a foot.

items.sentence: The baby slept.
items.question: Is the verb transitive or intransitive?
items.rule: Slept has no object, so it is intransitive.

items.sentence: The girl opened the window.
items.question: Is the verb transitive or intransitive?
items.rule: Opened has an object, the window, so it is transitive.

items.sentence: The birds flew away.
items.question: Is the verb transitive or intransitive?
items.rule: Flew has no object: away tells where, so the verb is intransitive.

items.sentence: He wrote a long letter.
items.question: Is the verb transitive or intransitive?
items.rule: Wrote has an object, a long letter, so it is transitive.

items.sentence: She was reluctant to speak, and looked at the floor until the teacher asked twice.
items.question: What does "reluctant" most likely mean here?
items.rule: She had to be asked twice, so she was unwilling.

items.sentence: Rain was scarce that year, and the wells nearly ran dry.
items.question: What does "scarce" most likely mean here?
items.rule: The wells nearly ran dry, so there was little rain.

items.sentence: The cat sat down upon the mat, and on its head it wore a ...
items.question: Which word most likely comes next?
items.rule: In a rhyme, the end of the line matches an earlier sound: mat, hat.

items.sentence: A hare laughed at a slow tortoise, so they agreed to race. The hare ran far ahead and lay down to sleep.
items.question: What most likely happens next?
items.rule: Stories of this shape turn on the proud one being caught out, so the slow one gets ahead.
right: The tortoise passes the sleeping hare.
wrong: The hare wins the race easily.
The tortoise goes home at once.

items.sentence: Once upon a time a poor woodcutter found a golden axe in the river.
items.question: What kind of text is this likely to be?
items.rule: Once upon a time, a poor man and a magical find are the shape of a folk tale.
right: A folk tale with a lesson

items.sentence: Up in the sky the kite flew high, it danced and dipped and waved ...
items.question: Which word most likely comes next?
items.rule: The rhyme with sky and high points to goodbye.

items.sentence: Meena said that she was hungry.
items.rule: In reported speech "I am" becomes "she was".

items.sentence: Ravi asked me where I was going.
items.rule: A reported question uses statement order and has no question mark.

items.sentence: Last week she said that she [will] visit us soon.
items.rule: In reported speech "will" becomes "would".

items.sentence: The teacher told us to open our books.
items.rule: An order is reported with "told" and "to".

items.sentence: The boy who won the race is my cousin.
items.rule: "Who" adds information about a person.

items.sentence: This is the book that I told you about.
items.rule: "That" adds information about a thing.

items.sentence: My brother and [me] went to the fair.
items.rule: As the subject, use "I": my brother and I went.

items.sentence: The teacher gave the prizes to Ravi and [I].
items.rule: After "to", use "me": to Ravi and me.

items.sentence: We painted the room [ourself].
items.rule: The reflexive form of "we" is "ourselves".

items.sentence: He cut [hisself] while peeling the mango.
items.rule: The reflexive form of "he" is "himself".

items.sentence: I hurt [me] when I fell off the bicycle.
items.rule: When the doer and the receiver are the same person, use the reflexive: myself.

items.sentence: The students finished [his] work early.
items.rule: A plural noun takes a plural pronoun: the students, their.

items.sentence: The puppy wagged [their] tail.
items.rule: One animal takes "its".

items.sentence: Meena and Ravi forgot [her] books.
items.rule: Two people joined by "and" take "their".

items.sentence: Yesterday she opened the door and [walks] in.
items.rule: "Yesterday" sets the past, so keep to it: opened, walked.

items.sentence: Last Sunday we went to the beach and [swim] all day.
items.rule: "Last Sunday" sets the past, so keep to it: went, swam.

items.sentence: Every day he picks up the bat and [hit] the ball.
items.rule: "Every day" sets the present, so keep to it: picks, hits.

items.sentence: The girl whose bag was lost is crying.
items.rule: "Whose" adds information about what belongs to a person.

items.sentence: The house where I was born is very old.
items.rule: "Where" adds information about a place.

items.sentence: I know the girl who painted this picture.
items.rule: "Who" adds information about a person.

items.sentence: She asked whether I had finished my work.
items.rule: A yes or no question is reported with "whether" or "if", in statement order.

items.sentence: Yesterday he said that he [can] swim across the lake.
items.rule: In reported speech "can" becomes "could".

items.sentence: When the bell rang, the children [run] out of the class.
items.rule: "Rang" sets the past, so keep to it: rang, ran.

items.sentence: The birds built [its] nest in our mango tree.
items.rule: A plural noun takes a plural pronoun: the birds, their.

items.sentence: When it rained, we stayed inside.
items.rule: The main clause can stand alone as a sentence: we stayed inside. "When it rained" cannot.

items.sentence: Although she was tired, Meena finished her work.
items.rule: The main clause can stand alone: Meena finished her work. "Although she was tired" cannot.

items.sentence: The boy who won smiled proudly.
items.rule: The main clause is: the boy smiled proudly. "Who won" is a clause that only adds to "boy".

items.sentence: We will go out if the rain stops.
items.rule: The main clause can stand alone: we will go out. "If the rain stops" cannot.

items.sentence: The children played IN THE GARDEN.
items.question: Are the words in capital letters a phrase or a clause?
items.rule: A phrase has no subject with its own verb: in the garden.

items.sentence: The children played UNTIL THE SUN SET.
items.question: Are the words in capital letters a phrase or a clause?
items.rule: A clause has a subject and a verb: the sun set.

items.sentence: She spoke WITH GREAT CARE.
items.question: Are the words in capital letters a phrase or a clause?
items.rule: A phrase has no subject with its own verb: with great care.

items.sentence: I will wait IF YOU ARE LATE.
items.question: Are the words in capital letters a phrase or a clause?
items.rule: A clause has a subject and a verb: you are.

items.sentence: The wind whispered through the trees.
items.question: Which figure of speech is this?
items.rule: Personification gives a human action to a thing: the wind whispered.

items.sentence: The classroom was a zoo.
items.question: Which figure of speech is this?
items.rule: A metaphor says one thing is another, without like or as.

items.sentence: Seven silver swans swam silently.
items.question: Which figure of speech is this?
items.rule: Alliteration repeats the same first sound: seven silver swans.

items.sentence: Her smile was sunshine.
items.question: Which figure of speech is this?
items.rule: A metaphor says one thing is another: her smile was sunshine.

items.sentence: The stars danced in the sky.
items.question: Which figure of speech is this?
items.rule: Personification gives a human action to a thing: the stars danced.

items.sentence: The baker stopped making doughnuts, tired of the hole business.
items.question: Which figure of speech is this?
items.rule: A pun plays on two meanings or two words that sound alike: hole and whole.

items.sentence: A letter to the head teacher asking for a day off.
items.question: Which sentence fits?
items.rule: A formal letter uses polite, complete and exact language.
right: I request you to grant me leave for one day.
wrong: Give me a day off, okay?

items.sentence: A message to a close friend about a film.
items.question: Which sentence fits?
items.rule: With a friend, friendly everyday language is right; stiff language sounds odd.
right: That film was great, you must see it!
wrong: I wish to inform you that the film was satisfactory.
Kindly be advised of the merits of the film.

items.sentence: A notice on the school board about a meeting.
items.question: Which sentence fits?
items.rule: A notice is formal: it gives what, where and when, plainly.
right: The meeting will be held in the hall at ten o'clock.
wrong: Hey guys, meeting in the hall, be there!
You lot had better turn up at ten.

items.sentence: A thank-you note to your grandmother.
items.question: Which sentence fits?
items.rule: A note to family is warm and polite: neither stiff nor curt.
right: Thank you so much for the lovely present.
wrong: Receipt of the present is hereby acknowledged.

items.sentence: It was raining. We went out.
items.question: Which sentence joins the two correctly?
items.rule: Although joins two ideas that pull apart; it is not used together with but.
right: Although it was raining, we went out.
wrong: Although it was raining, but we went out.
It was raining although we went out.

items.sentence: The boy won the prize. He is my cousin.
items.question: Which sentence joins the two correctly?
items.rule: Who joins a sentence about a person to the noun it describes.
right: The boy who won the prize is my cousin.
wrong: The boy is my cousin who he won the prize.
The boy which won the prize is my cousin.

items.sentence: She was tired. She finished her work.
items.question: Which sentence joins the two correctly?
items.rule: But joins two ideas that pull apart, making a compound sentence.
right: She was tired, but she finished her work.
wrong: She was tired, so she finished her work.
She was tired because she finished her work.

items.sentence: I missed the bus. I woke up late.
items.question: Which sentence joins the two correctly?
items.rule: Because joins a result to its reason.
right: I missed the bus because I woke up late.
wrong: I missed the bus, so I woke up late.
I missed the bus although I woke up late.

items.sentence: The house stood silent, its windows dark, and a cold wind rattled the gate.
items.question: What is the mood of these lines?
items.rule: Silent, dark, cold and rattled all build an uneasy mood.

items.sentence: Lanterns glowed along the street, drums rolled, and children raced past with sweets in their hands.
items.question: What is the mood of these lines?
items.rule: Lanterns, drums and children with sweets build a festive mood.

items.sentence: The swing hung still. Her shoes were by the door, where she had left them a year ago.
items.question: What is the mood of these lines?
items.rule: A still swing and shoes untouched for a year build a sad mood.

items.sentence: Of course the bus was late. It is always late on the one day I am early.
items.question: What is the tone of the speaker?
items.rule: Of course and always show a speaker who is mildly annoyed and joking about it.

items.sentence: First, wash the rice. Next, boil the water. Finally, add the rice and cover the pot.
items.question: How is this text built?
items.rule: First, next and finally mark steps in order.
wrong: As a problem and its answer
As a comparison of two things

items.sentence: The village well ran dry every summer. So the farmers dug a pond to store the rain.
items.question: How is this text built?
items.rule: The text states a problem, then what was done about it.
right: As a problem and its answer
wrong: As a comparison of two things

items.sentence: A bicycle costs little and needs no fuel, whereas a scooter is faster but costs more to run.
items.question: How is this text built?
items.rule: Whereas and but set two things side by side.
right: As a comparison of two things
wrong: As a problem and its answer

items.sentence: Heavy rain fell for three days. As a result, the river rose and the road was closed.
items.question: How is this text built?
items.rule: As a result links what happened to its cause.
right: As a cause and what followed from it
wrong: As a comparison of two things

items.sentence: "Take my umbrella," said Asha. "I can run home."
items.question: What does this show about the speaker?
items.rule: She gives up her own umbrella for someone else.

items.sentence: "I did not break it," said Vivek, looking at his shoes. "It was like that already."
items.question: What does this show about the speaker?
items.rule: Looking at his shoes while denying it suggests he is hiding something.
right: He is not telling the whole truth

items.sentence: "Let me try once more," said Meena, picking up the fallen blocks for the fifth time.
items.question: What does this show about the speaker?
items.rule: Trying a fifth time shows she does not give up.

items.sentence: "Naturally I came first," said Rohan. "I always do."
items.question: What does this show about the speaker?
items.rule: Naturally and I always do show someone who boasts.

items.sentence: The bridge was [build] many years ago.
items.rule: The passive uses the past participle: was built.

items.sentence: The letters were [wrote] by the secretary.
items.rule: The passive uses the past participle: were written.

items.sentence: The match was cancelled because of the rain.
items.rule: In the passive, the thing acted on comes first: the match was cancelled.

items.sentence: The results will be announced tomorrow.
items.rule: The future passive is will be with the past participle: will be announced.

items.sentence: If I [was] you, I would apologise.
items.rule: For something unreal, use were: if I were you.

items.sentence: If she had studied, she would have [pass] the test.
items.rule: After would have, use the past participle: would have passed.

items.sentence: If it rains tomorrow, we [would] cancel the picnic.
items.rule: A real possibility takes the present, then will: if it rains, we will cancel.

items.sentence: If I had known, I would have come earlier.
items.rule: For a past that did not happen: if with had, then would have.

items.sentence: Unless you hurry, you will miss the bus.
items.rule: Unless means if not: unless you hurry.

items.sentence: You should have [tell] me the truth.
items.rule: After should have, use the past participle: should have told.

items.sentence: He must have [forget] the meeting.
items.rule: After must have, use the past participle: must have forgotten.

items.sentence: They might have missed the last train.
items.rule: Might have with a past participle is a guess about the past.

items.sentence: She enjoys [swim] in the sea.
items.rule: After enjoy, use the -ing form: enjoys swimming.

items.sentence: He avoided [answer] the question.
items.rule: After avoid, use the -ing form: avoided answering.

items.sentence: I look forward to [meet] you.
items.rule: After look forward to, use the -ing form: to meeting you.

items.sentence: We agreed to meet at the station.
items.rule: After agree, use to with the verb: agreed to meet.

items.sentence: She likes reading, painting and [cook].
items.rule: Items in a list take the same form: reading, painting and cooking.

items.sentence: He spoke clearly, calmly and [confident].
items.rule: Items in a list take the same form: clearly, calmly and confidently.

items.sentence: The job needs patience, accuracy and good humour.
items.rule: Items in a list take the same form: three nouns.

items.sentence: I will call you WHEN I ARRIVE.
items.question: What does the clause in capital letters do?
items.rule: A clause that tells when, where, why or how is an adverb clause.
right: It tells when: an adverb clause
wrong: It describes a noun: an adjective clause
It is the thing known or said: a noun clause

items.sentence: The boy WHO WON THE RACE is my cousin.
items.question: What does the clause in capital letters do?
items.rule: A clause that describes a noun, here the boy, is an adjective clause.
right: It describes a noun: an adjective clause
wrong: It tells when: an adverb clause
It is the thing known or said: a noun clause

items.sentence: I know THAT SHE IS HONEST.
items.question: What does the clause in capital letters do?
items.rule: A clause that is the thing known, said or thought does the work of a noun.
right: It is the thing known or said: a noun clause
wrong: It describes a noun: an adjective clause
It tells why: an adverb clause

items.sentence: We stayed inside BECAUSE IT WAS RAINING.
items.question: What does the clause in capital letters do?
items.rule: A clause that tells why is an adverb clause.
right: It tells why: an adverb clause
wrong: It describes a noun: an adjective clause
It is the thing known or said: a noun clause

items.sentence: This is the house WHERE I WAS BORN.
items.question: What does the clause in capital letters do?
items.rule: Here the clause describes the house, so it is an adjective clause.
right: It describes a noun: an adjective clause
wrong: It tells why: an adverb clause
It is the thing known or said: a noun clause
